SITEMAP LASTMOD FRESHNESS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your sitemap's <lastmod> telling the truth?

Paste a sitemap.xml and check every <lastmod> date for the misconfigurations that quietly break the signal: an invalid or malformed date (the sitemap protocol requires a full W3C Datetime), a future-dated lastmod (impossible on its face), duplicate URLs with conflicting dates, and a suspiciously uniform date shared by nearly every URL — the "freshness-faking" pattern Google's own sitemap documentation warns can make it stop trusting the field entirely.

Nothing is uploaded. The XML you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device — see "Why can't the browser check the live pages too?" below for what the CLI adds.

1. Check a sitemap

2. Entries found

loclastmodFormatLive check

No <url> or <sitemap> entries found — is this a sitemap XML document?

Findings

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

The CLI fetches the sitemap and every URL's live headers over real HTTP — no cross-origin restriction, because it isn't a browser, and it only reads response headers, never the page body:

node check.mjs https://example.com/sitemap.xml --json
node check.mjs https://example.com/sitemap.xml --max-urls 200
node check.mjs https://example.com/sitemap.xml --uniform-threshold 0.8 --uniform-min-count 10

Get check.mjs, fetch-url.mjs, and engine.mjs from the repo — plain Node 18+, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the sitemap URL and the <loc> URLs that sitemap names — nothing goes through this site. Exit code 1 when a danger-severity finding is produced, the sitemap can't be fetched, or a URL's live headers can't be fetched (unverified is not the same as confirmed-clean).

What's checked

CheckWhat it flagsSeverityNeeds the CLI?
Invalid format<lastmod> isn't a valid W3C Datetime, or names a calendar date/time that doesn't exist (e.g. Feb 30)DangerNo
Future-dated<lastmod> is after today — never legitimateDangerNo
Duplicate / conflictingThe same <loc> listed twice — once harmlessly (same date) and once dangerously (different dates)Notice / DangerNo
Uniform patternA large share of URLs all claim the exact same date — the freshness-faking anti-patternNoticeNo
Server mismatchThe live page's own HTTP Last-Modified header doesn't confirm a change as recent as the sitemap claimsNoticeYes

More: why lastmod freshness matters, and the most common ways it breaks. See also: how this differs from XML-Sitemaps.com's free Sitemap Validator.

Common questions

What is sitemap "freshness faking"?

It's when a sitemap generator stamps every URL's <lastmod> with the current date on every build or deploy, regardless of whether the page actually changed — rather than only updating the date for pages with a real, significant content change. Google's own sitemap documentation says <lastmod> should reflect a genuine change, and that it may stop trusting a site's <lastmod> values if they consistently don't hold up, which defeats the entire point of having the field: helping a crawler prioritize what actually changed.

Why is a future-dated lastmod always wrong?

A page cannot have been last modified in the future — that's not a judgment call, it's a fact about time. A future <lastmod> is either a clock or timezone bug in whatever generated the sitemap (a server set to the wrong timezone can push a same-day timestamp past midnight UTC), or a placeholder value that was never replaced with the real date.

Why can't the browser check the live pages too?

A page's fetch() to a different origin either fails outright (in the default cors mode, if the target doesn't send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header naming this tool's origin) or succeeds as an opaque response (in no-cors mode) whose headers — including Last-Modified — cannot be read by JavaScript at all, by design. Either way, this page cannot reliably read a cross-origin page's own response headers unless that page's server opts in, which ordinary third-party sites have no reason to do. The zero-dependency CLI has no such restriction because it isn't a browser tab.

Is this a full technical-SEO audit?

No. It checks specific, mechanically verifiable properties of a sitemap's <lastmod> values — format validity, plausibility, internal consistency, and (via the CLI) agreement with each page's own HTTP headers. It is not a crawl of your whole site, not a ranking guarantee, and not a determination that your sitemap is otherwise correct.

It reports whether the sitemap you provided satisfies specific, mechanically checkable rules about its <lastmod> values — nothing more. It is not a ranking guarantee and not a full technical-SEO audit. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything you paste runs in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over the same sitemap: Canonical Tag Checker checks which URL a page's own rel=canonical link names as authoritative. AI Crawler Access Check checks whether your robots.txt actually allows the crawlers you think it does. Structured Data Drift Check checks whether a page's JSON-LD still says what its visible text says. And before any of those matter, Subpath Robots Check answers whether your sitemap is ever read at all — a site published under a URL subpath cannot govern its own robots.txt, so the Sitemap: line in it is never seen.

vs-xml-sitemaps-validator.html.text:
← Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check

Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check vs. XML-Sitemaps.com's Sitemap Validator

XML-Sitemaps.com's Sitemap Validator is a well-known free tool in the SEO community for checking a sitemap.xml file's own structure: is it well-formed XML, does it declare the right namespace, are the required tags present, and does it stay within the sitemap protocol's size and URL-count limits. For catching a hand-edit or a generator bug that produced broken XML, it is a solid, established first check.

Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check assumes your XML is already structurally fine and checks a completely different property: whether the <lastmod> values themselves are telling the truth. A sitemap can be perfectly valid XML — every tag closed, every namespace correct — and still have every single <lastmod> set to today's date regardless of whether the page changed, or set to a date in 2099, or list the same URL twice with two different dates. None of that is an XML-schema violation, so a schema validator has no reason to flag it — and this tool exists specifically for that gap.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I just generated or hand-edited a sitemap.xml and want to know if the XML itself is valid. XML-Sitemaps.com's Sitemap Validator — structural/schema validation is its job.
My sitemap validates fine, but I suspect the <lastmod> dates are wrong, uniform, or fake. Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check — this is exactly the property a schema validator does not look at.
I want to know if a URL's <lastmod> claim is actually confirmed by the live page. Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check's CLI — node check.mjs <sitemap-url> fetches each URL's real HTTP Last-Modified header and cross-checks it. A schema validator has no live-page step at all.
I want this checked automatically on every build, before it ships. Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check's CLI exits non-zero on a finding, wireable into any CI as an ordinary step, with no account or hosted service in the loop.

Neither tool replaces the other. Run a schema validator first if you have any doubt the XML itself is well-formed — a broken sitemap will confuse both tools and every crawler equally. Once the structure is confirmed sound, this tool answers the question a schema check was never built to ask: do the dates inside it actually mean anything?

Common questions

Should I use Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check or XML-Sitemaps.com's Sitemap Validator?

Different jobs, and many sites need both. XML-Sitemaps.com's Sitemap Validator checks that your sitemap.xml is well-formed and structurally correct per the sitemap protocol's XML schema — the right first check for a newly generated or hand-edited sitemap. Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check assumes the XML is structurally fine and checks a different property entirely: whether the <lastmod> dates inside it are individually valid, internally consistent, plausible, and (via the CLI) actually confirmed by each page's own HTTP Last-Modified response header.

Does XML-Sitemaps.com's validator check lastmod freshness or the freshness-faking pattern?

Based on its own public description, its Sitemap Validator checks XML syntax and schema conformance — structure, not the semantic plausibility of individual field values across the file, and it does not fetch each listed URL's own page to cross-check the date against reality. It is a schema validator, not a lastmod-truthfulness checker, which is a different and narrower job than this tool does.

Is XML-Sitemaps.com's tool free?

Yes, based on its own public listing — the Sitemap Validator needs no account for a basic check. Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check is also free, with no account, and the two are not competing on price — the difference is what each one actually checks.

Is this page affiliated with XML-Sitemaps.com?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by XML-Sitemaps.com. XML-Sitemaps.com and its Sitemap Validator are named here only to describe what that tool does and how it differs from this one, based on its own public description.

why-sitemap-lastmod-matters.html.text:
← Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check

Why sitemap lastmod freshness matters

Google's Search Central documentation on building a sitemap is direct about this: the <lastmod> field should name the date a page was last significantly modified, and the field is only useful to a crawler if it can be trusted. Google's own guidance says that when a site's lastmod values consistently don't hold up, it may choose to disregard the field for that site going forward — not just for the one wrong entry, but as a general policy toward a source that has proven unreliable.

That is a quiet failure, the same shape as a broken hreflang set: the sitemap still validates, the XML is still well-formed, and nothing in an ordinary QA pass shows anything wrong. The only symptom is that a crawler stops prioritizing your recently-changed pages the way the field was supposed to let it — because it decided the field was noise.

The pattern that causes this: freshness faking

Almost never intentional. The most common cause is a sitemap generator or static-site build step that stamps every URL with the current build timestamp by default, rather than the page's actual last-edited date — so a page nobody has touched in two years shows a <lastmod> of this morning simply because the site was redeployed. Run that build often enough and every single URL in the sitemap carries the same, constantly-advancing date, which is exactly the pattern that erodes trust in the field: a value that is always "today" carries no information about what actually changed. 

<!-- every one of 400 URLs, regenerated on every deploy -->
<url><loc>https://example.com/</loc><lastmod>2026-06-15</lastmod></url>
<url><loc>https://example.com/about</loc><lastmod>2026-06-15</lastmod></url>
<url><loc>https://example.com/blog/post-from-2019</loc><lastmod>2026-06-15</lastmod></url>
<!-- ...397 more, all dated today, regardless of when the page last changed -->

A second common cause is a CMS whose "last modified" timestamp updates on any save, including one that changed nothing meaningful — a draft re-save, a metadata-only edit, a cache-busting republish. The date is technically accurate about when a database row was touched, but not about when a reader would notice the page changed, which is the distinction Google's documentation is asking site owners to make.

The other checks this tool runs

  • Invalid format. The sitemap protocol requires a full W3C Datetime — a bare date or a full date-time with an explicit timezone. A bare time with no timezone, a slash-separated date, or a two-digit year all fail silently in some consumers rather than erroring loudly.
  • Future-dated. A page cannot have been modified in the future — always a clock/timezone bug or an unreplaced placeholder.
  • Duplicate or conflicting. The same URL listed twice with two different dates is a real conflict nothing consuming the sitemap can resolve on your behalf.
  • Server mismatch (CLI only). Whether the live page's own HTTP Last-Modified response header actually confirms a change as recent as the sitemap claims — reported as a signal to check, not proof, since some servers send render time rather than content-edit time, or send no such header at all.

Common questions

Where does Google say lastmod has to be accurate?

Google's Search Central documentation on building and submitting a sitemap describes <lastmod> as the date the page was last significantly modified, and says the field is only useful if it is accurate — and that a crawler which finds a site's lastmod values are not reliable may choose to disregard the field for that site going forward, rather than continuing to trust a signal that has proven wrong.

What actually happens if lastmod stops being trusted?

The entire point of lastmod is to help a crawler prioritize what to recrawl — a page that changed yesterday deserves attention sooner than one that hasn't changed in a year. If a crawler decides a site's lastmod values are not reliable, it loses that prioritization signal for every URL in the sitemap, not just the ones with a wrong date — a site with mostly-accurate dates and a handful of faked ones can lose the benefit for all of them, because the crawler has no cheap way to tell which entries to still trust.

How does freshness faking happen in practice?

Almost never on purpose. The most common cause is a sitemap generator or static-site build step that stamps every URL with the current build timestamp by default, rather than the page's actual last-edited date — so a page nobody has touched in two years shows a lastmod of this morning simply because the site was redeployed. A second common cause is a CMS whose "last modified" field updates on any save, including a save that changed nothing (a draft re-save, a metadata-only edit, a cache-busting republish).

Is a uniform lastmod always wrong?

No — a genuine one-time event, like a full site migration, a CMS re-platform, or a bulk content re-license, can legitimately touch every page on the same day. That is why this tool reports a uniform pattern as a notice-severity statistical signal rather than a certain violation: it names the pattern and the share of URLs involved, and leaves the judgment of whether it reflects a real event to the person who knows their own site's history.

Check your own sitemap: Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check. See also: how this differs from XML-Sitemaps.com's Sitemap Validator.
